extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical Greek drama and literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotelian criteria for what makes tragedy and comedy, including their origins, forms, metres, dramatic elements, and the nature of the laughable. Useful for literary analysis or historically informed creative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin in improvisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Both tragedy and comedy originated in improvisation (tragedy from the prelude to the dithyramb and comedy from the prelude to the phallic songs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle states 'At any rate it originated in improvisation—both tragedy itself and comedy.' This implies early dramatic forms grew out of communal, improvised ritual-song preludes, not from fully formed literary design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre choice follows poet's natural bent
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets were drawn by their natural bent towards one or the other (tragedy or comedy); some became writers of comedies instead of lampoons, others produced tragedies instead of epics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle suggests a creator's temperament or inclination determines suitable genre; selecting a genre contrary to one's bent is atypical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy as a higher art
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy (and by implication the more fully developed dramatic forms) is 'a higher kind of art and has greater value' than earlier or cruder forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a hierarchical evaluative claim: fully developed tragedy is of greater artistic value than precursor forms such as satyr plays or lampoons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development through progressive refinement of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy 'gradually evolved as men developed each element that came to light' and 'stopped when it had found its own natural form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good tragedy is the result of iterative development of constituent parts (actors, chorus, metre, spectacle); works that fail to integrate or develop these elements are less fully realized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase and arrangement of actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution of the number of actors improved the form (Aeschylus raised actors from one to two; Sophocles introduced three actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle highlights historical changes in actor numbers as formal advances—more actors allowed greater dialogue and dramatic complexity. Practical implication: distribution of speaking roles and interplay matters for dramatic effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curtailed chorus and primacy of dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Aeschylus 'curtailed the chorus and gave the dialogue the leading part.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective tragedy privileges dramatic dialogue over choral lyric; excessive choral dominance is a mark of less-developed drama. The chorus should support, not overshadow, the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction of scene-painting and spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophocles introduced scene-painting (and three actors), contributing to the craft and magnitude of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual staging ('scene-painting') and other embellishments are part of tragedy's maturation; they are components to be developed but are not substitutes for plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper metre for dialogue — the iambic
rubrics_metrics.description: When dialogue was introduced, 'Nature herself discovered the proper metre' — the iambic, because it is 'the most conversational of the metres.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues metre should suit function: iambic lines approximate everyday speech and are therefore appropriate for dialogue; trochaic and hexameter suit other uses (dance, elevated speech). Choosing an ill-suited metre is a formal flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of metre to origin forms (trochaic for satyrs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satyr plays used the trochaic tetrameter because their poetry suited Satyrs and was better for dancing; they were short and jocose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matched form and function: comic or dance-oriented interludes use metres suited to movement and jocularity. A mismatch (e.g., a serious scene in a dancing metre) undermines effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude and further embellishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters such as 'the number of acts' and further embellishments are features whose introduction and proper handling affect tragedy's development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes these are important but treats their detailed history as lengthy; nevertheless, scale (magnitude) and appropriate ornamentation are criteria for judging dramatic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy represents inferior people
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is 'a representation of inferior people' — not necessarily morally bad, but laughable as a species of the base or ugly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic subject is drawn from the 'inferior' class of human qualities; selecting characters and situations that expose that ludicrous inferiority is essential to comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the laughable — blunder or ugliness without pain
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable 'consists in some blunder or ugliness that does not cause pain or disaster' (example: the comic mask is ugly and distorted but not painful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For comedy to be proper, the perceived ugliness or mistake must be non-harmful; if the situation causes real pain or disaster it ceases to be comic. This distinguishes ridicule from cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity of comedy's formal history
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy's origins and stages are 'obscure because it was not at first treated seriously.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because comedy was less institutionalized early on, historical form-based prescriptions are fewer; practitioners should attend to comic effects (blunder, ridicule without harm) rather than strict historical conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satyr plays as late-developing antecedent to tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Being a development of the Satyr play, tragedy rose late from short plots and comic diction to full dignity; iambic replaced trochaic when dialogue was introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize satyr plays' features (short, jocose, dancing metre) as antecedents; serious tragedy achieves dignity by adopting conversational metres and expanded plot structure.
